# Review

Review code that is already checked out locally. Read source from the worktree; use `gh` only for
metadata and comments. Never fetch file contents through `gh`.

## Pick Mode

- **PR review:** use when inside a `pr-<number>` worktree, or the user says `review this PR` / `review PR #N`.
- **Landing review:** use when the user wants a final blocker check before push, merge, or PR creation.
- **Autoreview closeout:** use when the user asks for Codex/Claude/autoreview/second-model review, or after non-trivial edits before commit/ship.
- **Review wording:** use when the user wants a paste-ready GitHub comment or Smit-style review summary.
- **Maintainability:** read `references/modes/thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review/instructions.md` for the strict abstraction, file-growth, and branching-complexity lens.
- **Adversarial:** read `references/modes/interrogate/instructions.md` and its references for independent multi-model review and synthesis.
- **Entire history:** read `references/modes/entire-review/instructions.md` and its references before auditing a diff whose intent lives in checkpoints.

## Do

1. **Scope the diff** against the merge base, don't guess:
   `git diff --stat $(git merge-base main HEAD)..HEAD` then the full diff, plus
   `git log --oneline $(git merge-base main HEAD)..HEAD`. When the Entire Graph plugin is
   installed (`entire graph version` succeeds), add the entity-level view —
   `entire graph diff --base $(git merge-base main HEAD) --head HEAD --json` names the changed
   functions and types, and `entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text` checks a
   changed symbol's callers before judging its contract.
2. **For PR review, determine the PR number** from the branch (`git branch --show-current`, e.g. `pr-49207`).
   If the branch is not `pr-<number>`, ask or use `gh pr view` metadata.
3. **For PR review, read prior reviews first.** Fetch human and bot reviews (Copilot, CodeRabbit,
   `github-actions[bot]`). Note what is flagged, resolved, or ongoing. Commands: see
   `references/gh-commands.md`.
4. **Read code locally** (Read/Grep/Glob), full modified files, not just diff hunks. Never
   `gh api` for file contents.
5. **Check for real risks:** correctness, edge/error handling, codebase consistency, missing tests/docs,
   panic-prone code, secrets, destructive operations, injection risk, auth gaps, data loss, swallowed
   errors, debug artifacts, and source comments that contain process metadata.
6. **Route boundary-sensitive changes through the focused lenses.** Apply `correctness-review` when
   the diff touches persistence, lifecycle, hooks, locking, subprocesses, path ownership, or external
   tool state. Also apply `blast-radius` when it changes a shared lock, retry, context, subprocess,
   or environment helper. Fold their evidence-backed findings into this review rather than listing
   the same issue twice.
7. **Check extensibility:** flag hard-coded runtime, provider, language, model, or prompt assumptions
   unless the PR explicitly targets only that path. Prefer configuration, registries, adapters, or
   prompt templates when the system should stay open to more variants.
8. **Cross-reference prior feedback:** if a human or bot already raised a finding, note agreement or
   disagreement rather than re-raising it.
9. **Use Smit voice only when requested:** read `references/smit-review-voice.md` and output plain
   paste-ready comment text rather than the working-notes template.
10. **Present the summary**, then ask whether to submit via `gh` or keep as notes. Don't submit
   unprompted.

## Autoreview Closeout

Use the bundled structured review helper as an advisory second-model pass. Codex is the default engine
when none is set. Full helper details live in `references/autoreview-helper.md`.

```bash
<autoreview-helper> --mode local                          # dirty local patch only
<autoreview-helper> --mode branch --base origin/main      # branch/PR work
<autoreview-helper> --mode commit --commit HEAD           # already-committed/landed work
```

- Verify every accepted finding by reading the real code path before fixing it.
- Reject noise: unrealistic edge cases, speculative risks, broad rewrites, and unrelated refactors.
- If a fix changes code, rerun focused tests and rerun the helper until no accepted/actionable findings remain.
- Be patient. A run can take up to 30 minutes while the model is active.
- Do not push just to review. Push only on explicit request.

## Output

For working notes, use this template:

```text
## PR #<number>: <title>
### Summary        <1-2 sentences on what it does>
### Changes        <brief file-by-file or logical grouping>
### Prior Reviews  <who flagged what, and whether addressed; "No prior reviews." if none>
### Feedback       <numbered NEW findings with file:line; mark agree/build-on vs. new>
### Verdict        <approve | request changes | comment>
```

For landing review, use this template:

```text
Landing review
- Critical blockers:
- Non-blocking follow-ups:
- Tests or checks still worth running:
```

For autoreview closeout, include the command used, tests/proof run, findings accepted/rejected with
brief why, and the clean result from the final helper run.

Stop after presenting. Use local tools for all code/diffing; use `gh` only for PR title/body,
labels, linked issues, comments, and `gh pr checks <number>`.

## Code Review

I've reviewed the full diff against the latest `origin/main` (which the branch has been kept in sync with via merge commits). All CI checks pass, and I verified the new tests locally (`go test ./cmd/entire/cli/agent/...`). Here's my assessment:

### What works well

- **The AST guard is the right call.** `TestDeclaredCapsBuiltinListMatchesCapabilityHelpers` derives the built-in set from production code and cross-checks it against the `DeclaredCaps` doc comment, so the list can never silently rot again. This directly addresses the recurring drift that motivated the PR.

- **`builtinOnlyCapability[T]` is a clean extraction.** `AsLateTranscriptWriter` and `AsOutOfBandTokenSource` hand-rolled identical CapabilityDeclarer-exclusion logic; the new generic centralizes it and makes the pattern discoverable for future helpers.

- **Normalization is behavior-preserving.** `AsSidecarImageProvider`, `AsContextInjector`, `AsModelLister`, `AsStreamingTextGenerator`, and `AsPermissionConfigOwner` now use the standard resolver functions without changing their return values or declaration gating. The `AsPermissionConfigOwner` nil-safety improvement (old code would return `nil, false` on a nil interface already via Go's type assertion rules, but the explicit guard via `builtinCapability` aligns it with every other helper) is a consistency win.

- **Test coverage is solid.** Every normalized helper has characterization tests (nil agent, not-implemented, capability-declarer behavior), and `TestAsLateTranscriptWriter` properly tests the built-in-only exclusion gate.

### Minor observations (non-blocking)

1. **Commit history noise**: 7 out of 12 commits are upstream merge-sync commits. A squash merge would keep the main branch history clean; not blocking, just a merge-strategy note.

2. **`capabilityResolver` requires exactly one statement in the function body** (`len(fn.Body.List) != 1`). If a future helper adds a local variable or early validation before the return, the test would flag it as unresolved rather than as using the wrong resolver. That's a reasonable strictness tradeoff — it forces single-expression helper bodies — but worth being aware of. A future developer seeing an empty-resolver error might not immediately realize the fix is to keep the body a single `return` statement.

3. **`documentedBuiltinCapabilities` only looks in `capabilities.go`** (line `filepath.Join(findAgentDir(t), "capabilities.go")`), while `discoverCapabilityHelpers` scans every production `.go` file in the package. This is correct today because the doc comment lives on `DeclaredCaps` in `capabilities.go`, but if someone ever moves `DeclaredCaps` to another file, the test would break with a "DeclaredCaps type not found" failure — clear enough to fix.

### Verdict

# Run Playbook

A playbook is a plain markdown file listing an ordered sequence of actions for
one task shape. It is not auto-invoked. This router matches the task to a
playbook and copies its steps into a visible todo list so a step cannot quietly
disappear.

Commands may run inside the playbook after their own safety checks. A judgment
skill remains user-invoked: stop at that checkpoint, recommend the exact
`/skill-name`, and continue the playbook only after the user invokes it and the
checkpoint result is available.

## Available Playbooks

| Task shape | Playbook | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| Build a new feature | `playbooks/feature.md` | crosses a module boundary, introduces a new data shape, or scope is ambiguous enough to need a design doc |
| Fix a reported defect | `playbooks/bug-fix.md` | a bug that needs reproducing and root-causing, not an obvious one-liner |
| Ship a ready branch | `playbooks/ship.md` | work is done and committed, needs checking and a PR; `feature.md` and `bug-fix.md` reference this playbook as their final step |
| Review someone's PR | `playbooks/pr-review.md` | reviewing a PR, yours or another author's, before merge |
| Answer a read-only question | `playbooks/investigation.md` | how/why something works; deliverable is a cited answer, not a change |
| Restructure without changing behaviour | `playbooks/refactor.md` | rename, extract, inline, dedupe, move, or delete compat cruft |

If the task shape isn't in the table above, say so and proceed without a playbook. Do not invent
steps for a playbook that doesn't exist.

## Do

1. Match the task against the table above. If more than one playbook could apply, ask which task
   shape this is rather than guessing.
2. If nothing matches, tell the user and continue as an ordinary task -- do not fabricate a playbook.
3. Read the matched playbook file in full.
4. Copy every row into your todo list verbatim, in order, before doing any other
   work. One row = one todo item. Do not summarize, merge, or reorder.
5. Expand any playbook reference before starting. A row whose step reads `run playbooks/<name>.md`
   is a reference to another playbook, not a single step: read that file and splice its rows into
   the list in place of the reference, in order. Never copy a referenced playbook's rows back into
   the referring file -- the reference is what keeps one shipping sequence in one place. References
   expand one level only; a playbook that references itself is an error, so stop and say so.
6. Work the list top to bottom. Run `$ commands` directly when authorized. For a
   `/skill` checkpoint, stop and ask the user to invoke it; never load a user-only
   skill silently.
7. If a step doesn't apply, don't delete it -- mark it `skip: <reason>` and move on. Skipped steps
   stay visible in the final list, they don't disappear.
8. If a step says "repeat per task" (a loop), expand it into one todo item per actual task once
   that count is known (e.g. once `tasks.md` exists) -- not before.
9. Close with the playbook's **Reply:** contract. Each playbook names what to hand back; that
   contract is part of the playbook, not optional decoration.

## Output

A todo list matching the playbook's rows 1:1, with referenced playbooks and per-task loops expanded
in place, each item later marked done or `skip: <reason>`. The final response follows the matched
playbook's **Reply:** contract.

## Stop When

Every playbook step -- including the rows pulled in from a referenced playbook -- is done or
explicitly marked skipped, and the reply follows the playbook's **Reply:** contract. A step
silently missing from the final todo list means this failed.

# Review

Review code changes on the current branch by first reading checkpoint transcripts to
understand the intent behind each change, then auditing the actual diff for issues.
This produces an intent-aware review that catches mismatches between what the developer
wanted and what the code actually does.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Review:`

followed by a blank line, then the content.

- Apply the header to the **first response of the invocation only.** Do not re-print it on
  follow-up turns within the same invocation.
- Do **not** include the header on error or early-exit responses (e.g. "not a git repository",
  "no commits found between branch and base").

## Rules

1. This is a **read-only audit**. Do not modify any files during the review.
2. Always show a scope banner before findings so the user knows what is being reviewed.
3. If checkpoint context is unavailable, still perform the review using only the diff and
   commit messages. Clearly state that the review lacks intent context.
4. Group findings by file. Within each file, order by severity (Critical > High > Medium > Low).
5. Every finding must include a concrete suggestion or explanation, not just flag the issue.
6. After presenting findings, ask the user if they want a fix plan. Do not auto-fix.
7. Do not review generated files, lock files, or binary files unless the user explicitly
   asks for them.

## Process

### 1. Verify environment

Run `entire version` to check if the CLI is available. If it is not installed, note that
the review will proceed without checkpoint intent context (degraded mode).

### 2. Detect base ref

Find the mainline branch to diff against. Try these refs in order and use the first that
exists:

```bash
git rev-parse --verify origin/HEAD 2>/dev/null
git rev-parse --verify origin/main 2>/dev/null
git rev-parse --verify origin/master 2>/dev/null
git rev-parse --verify main 2>/dev/null
git rev-parse --verify master 2>/dev/null
```

If none exist, tell the user no base ref was found and ask them to specify one.

### 3. Compute scope

```bash
git rev-list --count <base>..HEAD
git diff --stat <base>..HEAD
```

Record the number of commits and files changed. This forms the scope banner.

### 4. Gather checkpoint intent (skip in degraded mode)

```bash
git log --format='%H%x00%s%x00%b' <base>..HEAD
```

Extract `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer values from commit bodies. Deduplicate checkpoint IDs.

For each unique checkpoint ID (up to 20):

```bash
entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <checkpoint-id> --json --no-pager
```

Parse the JSON to extract session metadata. For each non-review session in the checkpoint,
prefer the summary (intent + outcome). If no summary is available, fall back to the latest
user prompt. Truncate each checkpoint detail to 320 characters.

If `--json` fails for a checkpoint, fall back to the bare human-readable output:

```bash
entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <checkpoint-id> --no-pager
```

Do not use `--full` in the review workflow — it produces long narrative text harder for
agents to parse in bulk. If that also fails, skip the checkpoint and note it was unavailable.

Additionally, read the current in-progress session (if any) for uncommitted work context:

```bash
entire session current --json
```

If this returns valid JSON, extract `last_prompt` and `files_touched` — these represent
the intent behind uncommitted changes that are not yet captured in any checkpoint.

Build an intent map: for each file in the diff (committed + uncommitted), collect the
relevant intent context from all checkpoints and the active session that touched it.

### 5. Read the diff

When the Entire Graph plugin is installed (`entire graph version` succeeds), get the
entity-level change list first — it names exactly which functions and types changed,
which orders the file-by-file review and pairs each change with its checkpoint intent:

```bash
entire graph diff --base <base> --head HEAD --json
```

For any changed symbol whose contract matters, check callers before judging it:
`entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text`. Skip both silently when the
plugin is absent.

```bash
git diff <base>..HEAD
```

Also include uncommitted changes:

```bash
git diff HEAD
```

For large diffs (>5000 lines total), focus on the most critical files:
- Files with the most changes
- Files mentioned in checkpoint intents
- Source files over generated/config files

Read individual file diffs as needed rather than loading the entire diff at once.

### 6. Perform the review

Read the review rules:

```
references/review-rules.md
```

For each file in the diff, review it considering:

**With checkpoint context:**
- Does the implementation match the stated intent?
- Were the constraints from the transcript respected?
- Did the agent miss edge cases it discussed?
- Are there leftover debugging artifacts or TODOs?

**Always (with or without context):**
- Logic errors, off-by-one, null safety
- Security issues (injection, auth bypass, data exposure)
- Performance concerns (N+1 queries, unnecessary allocations)
- Error handling gaps
- API contract violations
- Dead code or unreachable branches

### 7. Output findings

Present findings using severity prefixes that align with the `entire review --fix` parser:

```
Entire Review:

Reviewing <branch> vs <base>: N commits, M files changed
[Intent context: available from K checkpoints | unavailable — reviewing diff only]

## path/to/file.ts

Critical: <issue description>
  Intent: <what the checkpoint said this should do, if available>
  Actual: <what the code actually does>
  Fix: <concrete suggestion>

High: <issue description>
  Intent: <what the checkpoint said this should do, if available>
  Actual: <what the code actually does>
  Fix: <concrete suggestion>

Medium: <improvement opportunity>
  Issue: <what is wrong>
  Fix: <concrete suggestion>

## path/to/other-file.ts

Low: <observation that is not a bug but worth noting>

---

Found N issues (X critical, Y high, Z medium, W low).
Would you like me to create a fix plan for the critical and high issues?
```

When checkpoint context is unavailable for a finding, omit the `Intent:` line and use
`Issue:` / `Fix:` instead.

### 8. Offer follow-up

After presenting findings, wait for the user's response:
- If they say yes to a fix plan, outline specific steps to address each critical/high issue.
- If they ask to fix directly, switch to implementation mode and address the issues.
- If they decline, the review is complete.

## Degraded Mode (no Entire CLI or no checkpoints)

When checkpoint context is unavailable:
1. Skip step 4 entirely
2. In the scope banner, state: "Intent context unavailable — reviewing diff only"

## Problem

`entire session attach <id> --agent opencode` fails with `transcript not found` for OpenCode sessions Entire never tracked — e.g. sessions spawned by an external session host rather than a hooked terminal. `resolveAndValidateTranscript` only calls `PrepareTranscript` when the transcript file *already exists* under `.entire/tmp`, on the assumption that preparation "can't conjure a file that was never started". For OpenCode that assumption is false: its transcript is produced on demand by `opencode export` (`fetchAndCacheExport`), which works for any session in the opencode store, tracked or not. OpenCode also lacks a `SessionBaseDirProvider`, so the project-dir fallback can't help. Net effect: no way to attach the correct session when hooks didn't capture one.

- New optional `TranscriptFetcher` agent capability (`agent.go` + `AsTranscriptFetcher`, type-assertion gated like `SidecarImageProvider`): the agent can materialize a session transcript on demand, including for sessions with no hook-cached file.
- `OpenCodeAgent.FetchTranscript` implements it via the existing `fetchAndCacheExport` (which already honors `ENTIRE_TEST_OPENCODE_MOCK_EXPORT`).
- `resolveAndValidateTranscript` consults the capability after the initial stat fails, before the project-dir search fallback. File-based agents are unaffected.

Out of scope (noted in the issue): `session list` enumeration from the opencode store — the attach path was the workflow blocker.

- New regression test `TestAttach_OpenCodeFetchesTranscriptForUntrackedSession`: a session with no hook-cached export attaches successfully via the fetch path (mock-export mode), producing session state with a checkpoint id.
- `TestFetchTranscript_ValidatesSessionID` / `TestFetchTranscript_AttemptsExport` for the new method.
- `go test ./cmd/entire/cli/...` and `golangci-lint run` clean.

The same scenario was exercised end-to-end against a real externally-hosted OpenCode session (`opencode export` succeeds, attach previously failed); with this change the fetch path materializes the transcript and attach proceeds.

# Thermo-Nuclear Code Quality Review

Use this skill for an unusually strict review focused on implementation quality, maintainability, abstraction quality, and codebase health.

Above all, this skill should push the reviewer to be **ambitious** about code structure. Do not merely identify local cleanup opportunities. Actively search for "code judo" moves: restructurings that preserve behavior while making the implementation dramatically simpler, smaller, more direct, and more elegant.

## Core Prompt

Start from this baseline:

> Perform a deep code quality audit of the current branch's changes.
> Rethink how to structure / implement the changes to meaningfully improve code quality without impacting behavior.
> Work to improve abstractions, modularity, reduce Spaghetti code, improve succinctness and legibility.
> Be ambitious, if there is a clear path to improving the implementation that involves restructuring some of the codebase, go for it.
> Be extremely thorough and rigorous. Measure twice, cut once.

## Non-Negotiable Additional Standards

Apply the baseline prompt above, plus these explicit review rules:

0. **Be ambitious about structural simplification.**
   - Do not stop at "this could be a bit cleaner."
   - Look for opportunities to reframe the change so that whole branches, helpers, modes, conditionals, or layers disappear entirely.
   - Prefer the solution that makes the code feel inevitable in hindsight.
   - Assume there is often a "code judo" move available: a re-organization that uses the existing architecture more effectively and makes the change dramatically simpler and more elegant.
   - If you see a path to delete complexity rather than rearrange it, push hard for that path.

1. **Do not let a PR push a file from under 1k lines to over 1k lines without a very strong reason.**
   - Treat this as a strong code-quality smell by default.
   - Prefer extracting helpers, subcomponents, modules, or local abstractions instead of letting a file sprawl past 1000 lines.
   - If the diff crosses that threshold, explicitly ask whether the code should be decomposed first.
   - Only waive this if there is a compelling structural reason and the resulting file is still clearly organized.

2. **Do not allow random spaghetti growth in existing code.**
   - Be highly suspicious of new ad-hoc conditionals, scattered special cases, or one-off branches inserted into unrelated flows.
   - If a change adds "weird if statements in random places", treat that as a design problem, not a stylistic nit.
   - Prefer pushing the logic into a dedicated abstraction, helper, state machine, policy object, or separate module instead of tangling an existing path.
   - Call out changes that make the surrounding code harder to reason about, even if they technically work.

3. **Bias toward cleaning the design, not just accepting working code.**
   - If behavior can stay the same while the structure becomes meaningfully cleaner, push for the cleaner version.
   - Do not rubber-stamp "it works" implementations that leave the codebase messier.
   - Strongly prefer simplifications that remove moving pieces altogether over refactors that merely spread the same complexity around.

4. **Prefer direct, boring, maintainable code over hacky or magical code.**
   - Treat brittle, ad-hoc, or "magic" behavior as a code-quality problem.
   - Be skeptical of generic mechanisms that hide simple data-shape assumptions.
   - Flag thin abstractions, identity wrappers, or pass-through helpers that add indirection without buying clarity.

5. **Push hard on type and boundary cleanliness when they affect maintainability.**
   - Question unnecessary optionality, `unknown`, `any`, or cast-heavy code when a clearer type boundary could exist.
   - Prefer explicit typed models or shared contracts over loosely-shaped ad-hoc objects.
   - If a branch relies on silent fallback to paper over an unclear invariant, ask whether the boundary should be made explicit instead.

6. **Keep logic in the canonical layer and reuse existing helpers.**
   - Call out feature logic leaking into shared paths or implementation details leaking through APIs.
   - Prefer existing canonical utilities/helpers over bespoke one-offs.
   - Push code toward the right package, service, or module instead of normalizing architectural drift.

7. **Treat unnecessary sequential orchestration and non-atomic updates as design smells when the cleaner structure is obvious.**
   - If independent work is serialized for no good reason, ask whether the flow should run in parallel instead.
   - If related updates can leave state half-applied, push for a more atomic structure.
   - Do not over-index on micro-optimizations, but do flag avoidable orchestration complexity that makes the implementation more brittle.

## Primary Review Questions

For every meaningful change, ask:

- Is there a "code judo" move that would make this dramatically simpler?
- Can this change be reframed so fewer concepts, branches, or helper layers are needed?
- Does this improve or worsen the local architecture?
- Did the diff add branching complexity where a better abstraction should exist?
- Did a previously cohesive module become more coupled, more stateful, or harder to scan?
- Is this logic living in the right file and layer?
- Did this change enlarge a file or component past a healthy size boundary?
- Are there repeated conditionals that signal a missing model or missing helper?
- Is the implementation direct and legible, or does it rely on special cases and incidental control flow?
- Is this abstraction actually earning its keep, or is it just a wrapper?
- Did the diff introduce casts, optionality, or ad-hoc object shapes that obscure the real invariant?
- Is this logic living in the canonical layer, or did the diff leak details across a boundary?
- Is this orchestration more sequential or less atomic than it needs to be?

## What to Flag Aggressively

Escalate findings when you see:

- A complicated implementation where a cleaner reframing could delete whole categories of complexity.
- Refactors that move code around but fail to reduce the number of concepts a reader must hold in their head.
- A file crossing 1000 lines due to the PR, especially if the new code could be split out.
- New conditionals bolted onto unrelated code paths.
- One-off booleans, nullable modes, or flags that complicate existing control flow.
- Feature-specific logic leaking into general-purpose modules.
- Generic "magic" handling that hides simple structure and makes the code harder to reason about.
- Thin wrappers or identity abstractions that add indirection without simplifying anything.
- Unnecessary casts, `any`, `unknown`, or optional params that muddy the real contract.
- Copy-pasted logic instead of extracted helpers.
- Narrow edge-case handling implemented in the middle of an already busy function.
- Refactors that technically pass tests but make the code less modular or less readable.
- "Temporary" branching that is likely to become permanent debt.
- Bespoke helpers where the codebase already has a canonical utility for the job.
- Logic added in the wrong layer/package when it should live somewhere more central.
- Sequential async flow where obviously independent work could stay simpler and clearer with parallel execution.
- Partial-update logic that leaves state less atomic than necessary.

## Preferred Remedies

When you identify a code-quality problem, prefer suggestions like:

- Delete a whole layer of indirection rather than polishing it.
- Reframe the state model so conditionals disappear instead of getting centralized.
- Change the ownership boundary so the feature becomes a natural extension of an existing abstraction.
- Turn special-case logic into a simpler default flow with fewer exceptions.
- Extract a helper or pure function.
- Split a large file into smaller focused modules.
- Move feature-specific logic behind a dedicated abstraction.
- Replace condition chains with a typed model or explicit dispatcher.
- Separate orchestration from business logic.
- Collapse duplicate branches into a single clearer flow.
- Delete wrappers that do not meaningfully clarify the API.
- Reuse the existing canonical helper instead of introducing a near-duplicate.
- Make type boundaries more explicit so the control flow gets simpler.
- Move the logic to the package/module/layer that already owns the concept.
- Parallelize independent work when that also simplifies the orchestration.
- Restructure related updates into a more atomic flow when partial state would be harder to reason about.

Do not be satisfied with "maybe rename this" feedback when the real issue is structural.
Do not be satisfied with a merely cleaner version of the same messy idea if there is a plausible path to a much simpler idea.

## Review Tone

Be direct, serious, and demanding about quality.
Do not be rude, but do not soften major maintainability issues into mild suggestions.
If the code is making the codebase messier, say so clearly.
If the implementation missed an opportunity for a dramatic simplification, say that clearly too.

Good phrases:

- `this pushes the file past 1k lines. can we decompose this first?`
- `this adds another special-case branch into an already busy flow. can we move this behind its own abstraction?`
- `this works, but it makes the surrounding code more spaghetti. let's keep the behavior and restructure the implementation.`
- `this feels like feature logic leaking into a shared path. can we isolate it?`
- `this abstraction seems unnecessary. can we just keep the direct flow?`
- `why does this need a cast / optional here? can we make the boundary more explicit instead?`
- `this looks like a bespoke helper for something we already have elsewhere. can we reuse the canonical one?`
- `i think there's a code-judo move here that makes this much simpler. can we reframe this so these branches disappear?`
- `this refactor moves complexity around, but doesn't really delete it. is there a way to make the model itself simpler?`

## Output Expectations

Prioritize findings in this order:

1. Structural code-quality regressions
2. Missed opportunities for dramatic simplification / code-judo restructuring
3. Spaghetti / branching complexity increases
4. Boundary / abstraction / type-contract problems that make the code harder to reason about
5. File-size and decomposition concerns
6. Modularity and abstraction issues
7. Legibility and maintainability concerns

Do not flood the review with low-value nits if there are larger structural issues.
Prefer a smaller number of high-conviction comments over a long list of cosmetic notes.

## Approval Bar

Do not approve merely because behavior seems correct.
The bar for approval is:

- no clear structural regression
- no obvious missed opportunity to make the implementation dramatically simpler when such a path is visible
- no unjustified file-size explosion
- no obvious spaghetti-growth from special-case branching
- no obviously hacky or magical abstraction that makes the code harder to reason about
- no unnecessary wrapper/cast/optionality churn obscuring the real design
- no clear architecture-boundary leak or avoidable canonical-helper duplication
- no missed opportunity for an obvious decomposition that would materially improve maintainability

Treat these as presumptive blockers unless the author can justify them clearly:

- the PR preserves a lot of incidental complexity when there is a plausible code-judo move that would delete it
- the PR pushes a file from below 1000 lines to above 1000 lines
- the PR adds ad-hoc branching that makes an existing flow more tangled
- the PR solves a local problem by scattering feature checks across shared code
- the PR adds an unnecessary abstraction, wrapper, or cast-heavy contract that makes the design more indirect
- the PR duplicates an existing helper or puts logic in the wrong layer when there is a clear canonical home

If those conditions are not met, leave explicit, actionable feedback and push for a cleaner decomposition.

# Blast Radius

Find what a change breaks somewhere else, before it ships.

Companion to `research-codebase` and `what-happened`. `research-codebase` tells
you what the code does. `what-happened` recovers why it is shaped that way.
Blast radius tells you what it breaks somewhere else.

Listing the callers is not the job. You can grep those in a second. The job is the breakage grep
won't show you.

## Use When

- The user asks for the blast radius of a change, or what it could break.
- You are reviewing a small diff you don't trust yet.
- A change touches a shared path, a wire format, or a dependency you don't own.

## Don't Trust Your Own Writeup

A blast-radius writeup that sounds right is worthless. It reads as convincing whether or not it's
true, and that is the trap. Don't hand back the writeup. Find the one or two facts the whole thing
depends on and prove them by running code. Words are where you start, not what you ship.

### How Sure Are You

For each fact the change's safety depends on, get it as far down this list as is cheap, and say
where it stopped.

1. You said so. Worthless on its own.
2. You pointed at the line. A real `file:line`, or the library's own source.
3. You showed the bad case can't happen. You walked the failure step by step and it doesn't reach.
4. You ran it. A script or test that calls the real code and fails loud if you're wrong.
5. You reproduced it in the running app.

Any safety fact you can't get to step 4, say so out loud. Don't write it up as settled. Step 4 is
usually one small script that imports the same library the app ships and calls the exact function
you're worried about.

## Do

1. **Read the change.** The diff, the symbols it adds, changes, and deletes, and what it now does
   differently, including the part the diff doesn't spell out. Pull the surrounding history with
   `git log -p $(git merge-base main HEAD)..HEAD` and `gh pr view` when a PR exists.
1b. **Sweep the mechanical radius with the graph when installed** (`entire graph version`
   succeeds). One call per changed symbol replaces the caller grep and adds what grep misses
   structurally — type consumers, data flows, co-change files:
   `entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text`. For a branch-wide change list,
   `entire graph diff --base <base> --head HEAD --json`. Graph output is evidence, not an
   oracle — it can miss callers (dynamic dispatch, interfaces), so it bounds step 3, never
   replaces it.
2. **Find the one fact it's safe because of.** Most changes that look scary are safe because of a
   single fact, like "this call only drops already-dead cache entries and does nothing else". Find
   that fact. If it holds, most of the scary cases die at once. Spend your time here, not on a long
   list of maybes.
3. **Look where grep stops.** Read the source of the library you call, and check its pinned version
   and any local patch. Work out when things run: microtasks, unmount and teardown, framework
   scheduling differences. Follow what a symbol search misses: the JSON an API returns, a DB column,
   a wire format, another language reading the same bytes, a feature flag, code three hops downstream.
4. **Audit semantic callers of shared primitives.** When a lock, retry, context, subprocess, or
   environment helper changes, compare callers with a deadline, cancellation without a deadline,
   and neither. Trace blocking, fairness, error identity, cleanup, inherited environment, and the
   outermost workflow result. Symbol callers are not enough when the changed contract is scheduling
   or process behavior.
5. **Be honest about each risk.** Give it a real chance of happening and a real cost if it does.
   Keep the risks you confirmed; list the ones you checked and cleared separately. Cite a real
   `file:line`. A search that finds nothing is still an answer. Never make up a caller or an API.
6. **Prove the one fact.** Write a script or test that runs the real code, run it, and paste what
   happened. If you can't prove it cheaply, mark it unproven. Don't round up.
7. **For a big or wide change, run it as an `arena`.** Ask several models the same question and merge
   the answers. Different models catch different real bugs.

## Output

- **What it does.** What changed, including the part that isn't obvious.
- **The one fact it's safe because of.** State it, say which step you got it to, and show the proof.
  If you couldn't prove it, write unproven.
- **Risks.** Only the real ones. Each names how it breaks, the `file:line`, how likely and how bad,
  and how to check. Paste the proof for the ones that matter.
- **Cleared.** What you checked and why it's fine.
- **Before you merge.** The cheapest test or repro that catches the real bug, including the script
  you wrote.

Write it through `unslop`, cite real code, and strip anything private before it goes anywhere public.

## Stop When

The one safety fact is either proven at step 4 or explicitly marked unproven. A writeup that
asserts safety without naming which step its central fact reached means this failed.

**What it does.** Seven `As*` helpers change how they work inside, but their signatures stay the same:
- `AsLateTranscriptWriter` and `AsOutOfBandTokenSource` move onto the new `builtinOnlyCapability`.
- `AsSidecarImageProvider`, `AsContextInjector`, `AsModelLister`, and `AsPermissionConfigOwner` move onto `builtinCapability`.
- `AsStreamingTextGenerator` moves onto `declaredCapability`.

The `DeclaredCaps` struct changes only in its doc comment. Its fields and JSON tags, which make up the external-agent protocol, are untouched.

**The one fact the change's safety depends on:** for every possible agent input, each of the seven helpers returns the same `(value, ok)` as before, including what's in `value` when `ok` is false. **Confirmed at step 4 (I ran it).**

I put a test in the scratchpad and added it to the package with `go test -overlay`, so no repository file was touched. The test copies the seven pre-PR implementations exactly from `upstream/main` `5893658fc`. It then runs old and new side by side for 15 kinds of agent:
- a nil interface;
- typed-nil pointers, for both a plain agent and an external one;
- a plain agent with no capabilities;
- an external agent that declares nothing, and one that declares streaming;
- a built-in and an external version of each capability.

**What it does:** it runs several reviewer agents against a branch at the same time. A separate "judge" agent then combines their reports into one verdict. The verdict is saved locally, or to a Trail if you choose. You can browse past results later with `entire review --findings`.

- Pass `--base upstream/main`. The default base is `origin/HEAD`, and your `origin` is your fork, so the comparison would start from the wrong place.
- It costs money: it launches several paid agent runs at once. Run `entire review --show-config` first if you want to see exactly what it would load. That option is read-only and free.

content.text:
Your teammate is right on all four points. Two of them are partly overstated, but there's enough here that my earlier "ready to merge" verdict was wrong. I also need to correct something I told you. In the review and blast-radius steps I said no production code bypasses the helpers. That search only covered the 22 built-in-only interfaces. It missed the bypass in claim 2 and the interfaces that have no `As*` helper at all.

## Claim by claim (checked at PR head `b79d170e0`)

**1. The guard misses capabilities that callers type-assert directly. Valid, but slightly overcounted.** Eight interfaces in package `agent` have no `As*` helper. Five of them are real optional capabilities that the documented list should cover:

| Interface | Asserted at |
|---|---|
| `SkillDiscoverer` | `review/picker.go:836`, `:1146` |
| `RestoredSessionPathResolver` | `strategy/manual_commit_pending.go:391` |
| `HookConfigLocator` | `agent/registry.go:260` |
| `ProtectedFilesProvider` | `agent/registry.go:291` |
| `SessionFileCandidatesProvider` | `agent/session_store.go:185` |

The teammate overcounted with these three:
- `SessionLocator` (`session_store.go:39`) is just the narrow set of methods the session store needs. It isn't an optional capability.
- `TestOnly` is a marker the registry checks. It isn't a capability either.
- `FileWatcher` is never type-asserted in production code, only in a test. It's effectively dead.

So the teammate's suggested "list every interface" test would need an exclusion list of its own.

**2. A call site skips the declaration check. Valid, and the bug predates this PR.** `manual_commit_pending.go:473` does `sessionAgent.(agent.PromptExtractor)` directly. The external adapter always implements `ExtractPrompts` (I confirmed this from its method set), so an external agent that declared `transcript_analyzer: false` still gets its prompts extracted when a session is restored. The impact is small: the result is only a prompt preview, and any error is swallowed. But it is a real bypass of the declaration check, and upstream `main` has the same line.

**3. Some comments now say the opposite of what the code does. Valid, and this PR made it worse.**
- `inject.go:45`: this PR wrote "Context injection is built-in only" (commit `52374d422`), but the helper uses `builtinCapability`, which accepts external agents.
- `capabilities.go:4`: the doc says an agent must "both implement … AND declare". That isn't true for the 22 helpers that need no declaration.
- The underlying cause is bigger than those two lines. About a dozen existing comments use "built-in only" to mean "has no external-protocol declaration" (for example `capabilities.go:110`, `:209`, `:280`–`:310`, and `caller_session.go:27`). By naming the new function `builtinOnlyCapability`, this PR gave the phrase a stronger meaning: "refuses external agents". Every one of those older comments now reads as wrong.

**4. The guard can't tell the two built-in resolvers apart. Valid.** I listed this as Low ("the list doesn't show which entries refuse external agents"). The teammate's framing is the better one. Switching `AsOutOfBandTokenSource` or `AsLateTranscriptWriter` to plain `builtinCapability` would still pass the guard, and those two are exactly the security-relevant helpers. Only their unit tests would catch it.

## Proposed fix (needs your approval before I edit)

These all belong in this PR, because they're gaps in the guard the PR exists to add:

1. **Rename `builtinOnlyCapability` instead of rewording a dozen comments.** A name like `refuseDeclarersCapability` says what it does, and the existing "built-in only" comments go back to being correct. Then fix `inject.go:45` and the `CapabilityDeclarer` doc at `capabilities.go:4` so they describe the three resolvers accurately.
2. **Mark the refusing entries in the documented list**, for example `- LateTranscriptWriter (refuses external agents)`. The test then checks that each marker matches the function the helper actually uses.
3. **Add `As*` helpers for the five real capabilities, and switch their eight call sites to use them.** Add a `testutil.GitGrepGuard` that fails on any `.(agent.<Interface>)` type assertion outside package `agent`. That guard covers claim 2: `manual_commit_pending.go:473` switches to `AsPromptExtractor`. Exclude `SessionLocator` and `TestOnly` by name.

**The tradeoff in item 3:** it touches `review/`, `strategy/`, `registry.go`, and `session_store.go`, so the PR grows beyond the `agent` package and fixes a bug that predates it. The narrower alternative is to do items 1 and 2 plus the five list entries now, and move claim 2 and the grep guard to a separate PR. I recommend the full version. A guard that's blind to direct type assertions is the same drift problem the PR was opened to stop, and the claim 2 fix is one line once the guard exists.

`DeclaredCaps` documents the capabilities that agents can have without declaring them through `DeclaredCapabilities`. That list had fallen out of date more than once, and some callers skipped the `As*` helpers entirely by type-asserting agents directly, which also skipped the declaration check.

This PR makes the list and the helpers enforceable, so reviewers no longer have to keep them in sync by hand.

## What changed

Every package-level `As*` capability helper now resolves through one of three standard functions:

- `declaredCapability`: a `CapabilityDeclarer` must implement the interface and declare the matching `DeclaredCaps` field.
- `builtinCapability`: implementing the interface is enough; there is no `DeclaredCaps` field to check.
- `nonDeclarerCapability`: `CapabilityDeclarer` agents are refused even if they implement the interface (`LateTranscriptWriter`, `OutOfBandTokenSource`).

`nonDeclarerCapability` replaces two hand-written copies of the same logic. Five existing helpers moved onto the standard functions without changing their signatures, and five new helpers replace direct type assertions: `AsSkillDiscoverer`, `AsRestoredSessionPathResolver`, `AsProtectedFilesProvider`, `AsHookConfigLocator`, and `AsSessionFileCandidatesProvider`.

## Guards

- An AST test checks that every `As*` helper uses one of the three functions, that the list above `DeclaredCaps` (now 27 entries) exactly matches the `builtinCapability` and `nonDeclarerCapability` helpers, that it is sorted, and that the entries marked `(refuses CapabilityDeclarer agents)` are exactly the `nonDeclarerCapability` helpers.
- A `testutil.GitGrepGuard` test fails on any type assertion or type-switch case that names a capability interface from package `agent`, so callers have to go through the helper and its declaration check. `Agent`, `CapabilityDeclarer`, `SessionLocator`, and `TestOnly` are allowed, each with a stated reason.

## Behavior change

Restoring a session (`manual_commit_pending.go`) previously type-asserted the agent to `PromptExtractor` directly. External agents always implement `ExtractPrompts`, so an external agent that declared `transcript_analyzer: false` still had its prompts extracted for the restore preview, which also ran its `extract-prompts` subcommand. It now goes through `AsPromptExtractor` and respects the declaration. This bug predates this PR. The guard above is what found it.

All other helpers return the same values as before. `AsProtectedFilesProvider` keeps accepting external agents, because the external adapter forwards `ProtectedFiles` from the agent's info response.

There are no public API or protocol-schema changes.
